applicableAreas: Site perimeter along property boundaries where electric easements are located
findings.observation: Examined Site Plan (Sheet 9) and Electrical Design Plan (Sheet 21). Vision analysis confirms that buildings are dimensioned from property lines (e.g., Bldg 5 shown as 19.3' from top property line, Bldg 6 shown as 21.3' from right property line), but NO explicit clearance dimensions are drawn from easement boundaries to proposed structures. Electric and PUE boundaries are shown with dashed lines on the site plan, but distance from easement boundaries to buildings or structures is not dimensioned or verified. The easement boundaries are delineated but clearance verification is absent. Existing trees overlap OHE lines along the southern boundary.
findings.reasoning: UCM § 1.16.0 requires that 'Easements are clearly delineated on plans, with surveys showing proximities' to structures. The deficiency here is that while easement boundaries are shown on the site plan, the specific clearance distances from those boundaries to proposed structures are not dimensioned or documented. For overhead distribution facilities requiring 15-foot clearance and underground facilities requiring 5-foot clearance per UCM § 1.10.3, the applicant must provide explicit dimensional verification that clearances are maintained. The distance-to-property-line approach is insufficient because the easement boundaries may not align with property lines. Additionally, existing trees visible on the vision analysis overlap the OHE lines, indicating potential ground-to-sky clearance violations that further underscore the need for clearance verification exhibits.
findings.comment: Clearance verification exhibits do not show existing electric easements with dimensions from easement boundaries to proposed structures. Easement boundaries are shown on the site plan but distances from easement boundaries to buildings are not dimensioned. Provide dimensional clearance exhibits showing distances from all electric easement boundaries to proposed structures, confirming minimum 15-foot clearance for overhead distribution facilities and 5-foot clearance for underground facilities.

findings.observation: Vision analysis of Site Plan (Sheet 9) and Electrical Design Plan (Sheet 21) reveals the following easement labels: 'Top boundary: 5' P.U.E. Vol. 69, Pg. 14 Vol. 73, Pg. 76 P.R.T.C.T.x.'; 'Right boundary (upper): 5' Electric Easement Vol. 69, Pg. 14 Vol. 73, Pg. 76 P.R.T.C.T.x.'; 'Right boundary (lower): 5' Elec. Easement Vol. 69, Pg. 14 Vol. 73, Pg. 76 P.R.T.C.T.x.'; 'Far right edge (bottom): 5' Elec. & Tele. Easement Vol. 5068, Pg. 883 D.R.T.C.T.x.' All easement labels use abbreviated nomenclature ('Elec.' instead of 'Electric', 'Tele.' instead of 'Telecommunications', 'P.U.E.' instead of full spelling) rather than complete proper nomenclature.
findings.reasoning: UCM § 1.16.0 requires that 'Easements are clearly delineated on plans' with proper nomenclature and designations. The grouping's regulatory overview explicitly states: 'Plans must explicitly designate easements...generic easement labels are insufficient.' The use of abbreviated forms ('EE,' 'ETE,' 'Elec.') violates this requirement because abbreviated forms do not clearly communicate the full scope of utilities authorized within the easement. Complete proper nomenclature such as 'Electric distribution, electric telecommunications, and electric fiber easement' ensures clarity about which utilities are present and their respective clearance requirements. Abbreviations create ambiguity about facility types and can lead to compliance verification errors.
findings.comment: Easement call-outs use abbreviated forms (e.g., 'Elec. Easement,' 'Elec. & Tele. Easement,' 'P.U.E.') rather than complete proper nomenclature. Revise all easement labels to use complete designations, for example: 'Electric distribution, electric telecommunications, and electric fiber easement' or equivalent full nomenclature that clearly identifies all facilities authorized within each easement.

applicableAreas: Southern and western property boundaries where overhead electric (OHE) lines are located
findings.observation: Vision analysis of Site Plan (Sheet 9) and Electrical Design Plan (Sheet 21) reveals that overhead electric lines are depicted along the southern and western property boundaries, labeled as 'OHE' (Overhead Electric). The plans show these existing OHE lines running parallel to the property lines where electric easements are also delineated. However, the easement labels for these areas do not include the designation 'aerial electric easement.' Instead, the easements are labeled generically as '5' Electric Easement' and '5' Elec. & Tele. Easement' without the 'aerial' designation required when overhead facilities are present.
findings.reasoning: The regulatory overview explicitly states: 'Plans must explicitly designate easements as aerial when overhead facilities are present—generic electric easement labels are insufficient.' UCM § 1.3.24 addresses 'Easements for Electric Distribution Facilities' and requires that easements accommodate safe construction, operation, maintenance, and access. UCM § 1.16.0 requires clear delineation. When overhead facilities are present, the easement must be labeled 'aerial electric easement' to distinguish it from underground electric easements and to communicate the vertical clearance requirements (16 feet minimum for access, 7.5 feet horizontal sky-to-ground clearance per UCM § 1.10.3) that apply to aerial facilities. Generic labeling fails to communicate these critical distinctions.
findings.comment: Overhead electric facilities not designated with 'aerial electric easement' label; generic electric easement label used instead. Overhead electric lines are present along the southern and western property boundaries but are not identified as 'aerial electric easement.' Revise all easement labels to include 'aerial' designation where overhead conductors or facilities are present, for example: 'Aerial electric distribution, electric telecommunications, and electric fiber easement.'

applicableAreas: Public Utility Easements along property boundaries (north, east, southeast boundaries)
findings.observation: Vision analysis of Site Plan (Sheet 9) and Electrical Design Plan (Sheet 21) confirms that PUEs are shown along property boundaries: '5' P.U.E. Vol. 69, Pg. 14 Vol. 73, Pg. 76' on the northern boundary, '10' P.U.E.' on the western boundary, and '10' P.U.E. Vol. 69, Pg. 14 Vol. 73, Pg. 76' on the southern boundary. The electrical plan indicates that proposed 'Underground Electric Line' crosses through at least one of these PUEs. However, the site plan does not show detailed utility separation specifications or a utility separation table documenting the distances between the proposed electric facilities and any other utilities potentially located within the PUEs (water, wastewater, telecommunications, etc.). Without this utility coordination detail, it is unclear whether the 5-foot and 10-foot PUE widths are sufficient to accommodate all utilities with required minimum separation distances.
findings.reasoning: Without detailed utility coordination and separation distances documented on the plans, the adequacy of PUE widths cannot be determined. The applicant must provide a utility coordination analysis showing all utilities within each PUE and the minimum separation distances between them, confirming that the 5-foot, 7.5-foot, and 10-foot PUE widths are adequate for all proposed utilities.
findings.comment: Public Utility Easements (PUE) may not be wide enough to accommodate all proposed utilities with required separation distances. The site plan shows 5-foot, 7.5-foot, and 10-foot PUEs but does not provide utility separation specifications or a utility coordination table. Provide a detailed utility coordination analysis showing the location and horizontal separation distances of all utilities (electric, water, wastewater, telecommunications, etc.) proposed within each PUE, verifying that PUE widths are adequate.

applicableAreas: Electric transformer pad locations; eastern property line easement area; site perimeter
findings.observation: Vision analysis of Electrical Design Plan (Sheet 21) and Site Plan (Sheet 9) confirms: (1) Two pad-mounted transformer pads are shown on the site, one on the west side and one on the east side. The plan note adjacent to the transformer pad states 'need to look up approp. detail,' indicating the access design is incomplete. (2) No dimensioned access routes are drawn from parking areas, public ROW, or driveways to either transformer pad. (3) Vision analysis of Site Plan (Sheet 9) shows an 'Existing Retaining Wall to be Replaced' and 'Wood Fence' running along the eastern property line where the electric easements are located, potentially obstructing access. (4) The General Notes (Sheet 3) specify that '24-hour access to electric facilities shall be maintained' and 'Vehicular access for Austin Energy trucks and equipment is always to be maintained within the easement,' but the site plan does not show how this requirement is being met. (5) No gates, lift gates, removable sections, or other 24/7 access provisions are noted on the plans.
findings.reasoning: UCM § 1.3.16 requires 'Truck access to AE Construction and Existing Facility Sites' and UCM § 1.14.4 addresses transmission access corridors with 24-hour access requirements. The regulatory overview specifies 'Standard distribution access: 12 feet minimum horizontal width, 16 feet vertical clearance' and 'All-weather surface definition: Hot mix asphaltic concrete (HMAC) or Portland cement concrete (PCC) pavement.' The applicant must demonstrate that maintenance vehicles can reach all electric facilities from the public ROW or parking areas. The incomplete transformer pad detail ('need to look up approp. detail') and the absence of dimensioned access routes are deficiencies. The existing retaining wall and fence shown on the eastern boundary where electric easements are located could obstruct access to those easements. Additionally, no notation of 24/7 access provisions (such as gates with AE locks) is shown, raising questions about access during off-hours.
findings.comment: 24/7 vehicular access to electric easements and facilities not provided or shown, including access routes from public right-of-way, or is obstructed by fencing, gates, security features, or other site improvements. Transformer pad detail is incomplete (noted as 'need to look up approp. detail'). Provide detailed access routes from public ROW and/or parking areas to all electric transformer pads and easements, with dimensions and surface specifications. Show how 24/7 access is maintained to all electric facilities, including provisions for gates, removable fencing, or other mechanisms that allow Austin Energy personnel access at any time. Clarify the status of the existing retaining wall and fence along the eastern easement boundary and confirm they do not obstruct utility access.

applicableAreas: Electric easement areas, particularly the 5-foot electric easements along eastern and southeastern property boundaries
findings.observation: Vision analysis of Grading Plan (Sheet 11) reveals that surface materials within electric easement areas are NOT explicitly specified or called out. The plan shows contour lines and spot elevations within the '5' Electric Easement' along the eastern boundary and the '5' Elec. & Tele. Easement' in the southeast corner, but no hatching, notation, or legend entry indicates whether these areas will be paved with HMAC or PCC concrete, or left unpaved (grass, gravel, or dirt). The Legend on Sheet 11 does not include surface material specifications for easement areas. The General Notes do not address surface specifications for electric easement areas. Vision analysis of electrical and site plans shows that existing trees and a wood fence occupy areas adjacent to or potentially within the easement boundaries, but there is no indication that maintenance vehicle access routes have been graded and paved.
findings.reasoning: UCM § 1.3.16 explicitly requires 'all-weather surface definition: Hot mix asphaltic concrete (HMAC) or Portland cement concrete (PCC) pavement capable of supporting 72,180 lbs total vehicle weight with maximum 32,530 lbs rear axle weight. Gravel, grass, and unpaved surfaces do NOT qualify.' LDC § 25-12-173 Section 202.1 defines an all-weather driving surface for maintenance access. The applicant must specify paved surfaces (HMAC or PCC) in all areas designated as electric easement or maintenance access corridors. Without this specification, there is no assurance that maintenance trucks and bucket trucks can access the easement. The narrow 5-foot easements with existing trees and fencing suggest that maintenance access has not been adequately planned.
findings.comment: Drivable surfaces within electric easements not suitable for maintenance vehicles and large bucket trucks; surfaces are unpaved, grass, gravel, or otherwise inadequate for heavy equipment. No surface material specification is provided for the 5-foot electric easements. Specify that all electric easement areas shall be graded and paved with HMAC or PCC concrete capable of supporting 72,180 lbs total vehicle weight. Provide a grading and paving plan for all electric easement access routes, showing the surface specification and confirming that maintenance vehicle access is maintained along the full length of easements.

applicableAreas: Southern property boundary where overhead electric (OHE) lines and existing trees are located
findings.observation: Vision analysis of Electrical Design Plan (Sheet 21) explicitly states: 'Existing tree symbols (large circles) do overlap the existing OHE (overhead electric) lines running along the southern boundary.' Vision analysis of Site Plan (Sheet 9) confirms existing trees are shown adjacent to the OHE lines along the southern property line. The Grading Plan (Sheet 11) shows contour lines and existing tree symbols in the area of the OHE lines. The General Notes (Sheet 3) require that 'Austin Energy has the right to prune and/or remove trees...to keep the easements clear' and state that 'Trees: Minimum 15 lateral feet from overhead conductors or equipment' (from the regulatory overview). The current condition shows existing trees overlapping or immediately adjacent to overhead electric lines.
findings.reasoning: UCM § 1.10.3 specifies 'Permanent Clearances From AE Overhead Distribution Lines and Facilities: 7.5 feet minimum horizontal sky-to-ground clearance from overhead conductors' and '15-foot radius clearance from overhead distribution primary and neutral conductors.' UCM § 1.10.10.2 addresses ground-to-sky clearances and customer activities in easements. The regulatory overview explicitly requires 'Trees: Minimum 15 lateral feet from overhead conductors or equipment.' The vision analysis documenting tree symbols overlapping OHE lines indicates that existing ground cover and trees are encroaching into the 15-foot clearance zone required by code. The site plan must demonstrate that existing trees and vegetation do not violate the 15-foot clearance requirement or be removed/pruned to comply.
findings.comment: Ground-to-sky clearances within electric easements and electric and telecommunications easements (ETE) not maintained; buildings, structures, utilities, site amenities, landscaping, trees, overhead features, or other improvements encroach from ground to sky. Existing trees overlap or are immediately adjacent to overhead electric lines along the southern property boundary, violating the minimum 15-foot lateral clearance required from overhead conductors. Provide a tree preservation and removal plan that either demonstrates 15-foot minimum clearance from overhead conductors will be maintained or identifies trees for removal/pruning to comply with clearance requirements.

applicableAreas: Public Utility Easements containing or adjacent to electric facilities (north, east, and southeast property boundaries)
findings.observation: Vision analysis of Site Plan (Sheet 9) shows PUEs along property boundaries and existing trees/landscaping nearby. The Landscape Plan (Sheet 31) shows landscaping features throughout the site. However, the site plan does not provide a detailed specification of which site amenities and landscaping will be placed within PUE boundaries versus outside them. The plans do not include notation of 'written Austin Energy approval' for any improvements within or near PUEs. The general notes do not address specific approvals for landscaping or other site improvements within PUEs. Without detailed improvements plan notes on the PUE areas, it is unclear whether final landscaping and site amenities will encroach into PUE boundaries without required written approval from Austin Energy.
findings.reasoning: UCM § 1.5.2.1.L requires that 'Customer facilities in easements require AE written approval.' UCM § 1.10.10.2 addresses customer activities in utility easements. The site plan must either show that no improvements are planned within PUE boundaries, or provide notation of written AE approval for any landscaping, trees, or other site amenities to be located within PUE areas. The lack of detailed specification about which improvements (if any) will be within PUEs creates ambiguity about compliance.
findings.comment: Public Utility Easements (PUE) not kept clear of buildings, structures, utilities, site amenities, landscaping, and other improvements. The site plan does not clearly specify which improvements (if any) will be placed within PUE boundaries, nor does it document written Austin Energy approval for any such improvements. Clarify which site amenities, landscaping, and other improvements will be located within PUE boundaries. If any improvements are proposed within PUEs, provide notation on the plans indicating written Austin Energy approval for those specific improvements.

applicableAreas: Parking areas and curbing along access routes to transmission easements
findings.observation: Vision analysis of Construction Details Sheet 22 confirms that laydown curb specifications (COA 430S-1) are available and shown on the details sheet. The sheet explicitly depicts 'LAYDOWN CURB' in the curb type panel. However, vision analysis also confirms that 'There are NO transmission-specific or electrical easement-specific curb details shown on this document.' The site plan does not explicitly call out or specify which curb types will be used in areas where vehicles access transmission easements. The General Notes (Sheet 3) state that 'Roads/driveways/pavement/parking within the easement should be built to support a 46,000 lb tandem axle (5 foot spacing)' and 'All curbing within the electric transmission easement must be over-roll curbing.' However, no site plan annotation indicates where transmission easements are located or whether laydown curbs are specified for those areas.
findings.reasoning: UCM § 1.14.4.E and 1.14.4.F address transmission easement access and curb specifications. SSM Item 430s specifies laydown curb construction. The grouping's regulatory overview states 'Inadequate curb specification: Detail sheets show standard curb along transmission easement access route instead of laydown curb rated for required loading.' While the construction details sheet includes laydown curb specifications, the site plan itself does not specify whether transmission easement access routes will use laydown curbs. The applicability of this item hinges on whether transmission easements exist on this site and whether parking or curbing are located along their access routes. The extensive transmission notes on Sheet 3 suggest transmission facilities may be present, but the site plan layout is unclear about transmission easement locations and curb specifications. This creates ambiguity.
findings.comment: Laydown curb rated to withstand required vehicle loading not provided for Austin Energy truck access where parking areas or curbing are located along access routes to transmission easements. While COA 430S laydown curb specifications are available, the site plan does not explicitly specify where laydown curbs will be used in transmission easement areas. Clarify whether transmission easements exist on this site. If transmission easements are present along or near parking or curb areas, specify that all curbing within transmission easement access routes shall be laydown curb (over-roll curb) rated for 46,000 lb tandem axle loading with 5-foot spacing per SSM Item 430s and UCM § 1.14.4.

applicableAreas: Entire site, if transmission easements are present
findings.observation: General Notes (Sheet 3) contain extensive transmission facility requirements, including: 'Do not dig or grade within 25 feet of transmission structures,' '25-foot clearance from energized transmission lines,' 'Roads/driveways/pavement/parking within the easement should be built to support a 46,000 lb tandem axle,' and specific requirements for access corridors, gates (minimum 16 feet wide, 24-hour access), grades (no slopes greater than 8%), curbs (laydown curbs), and drainage restrictions. These transmission notes indicate that transmission facilities are either present on or immediately adjacent to the site. However, examination of the Site Plan (Sheet 9), Electrical Design Plan (Sheet 21), and Grading Plan (Sheet 11) reveals NO 25-foot-wide access corridors with 16-foot vertical clearance explicitly shown or dimensioned. The electric easements shown on the plans are only 5-foot, 7.5-foot, and 10-foot wide—far below the 25-foot transmission requirement. No transmission easement access routes are labeled or dimensioned with 25-foot widths.
findings.reasoning: UCM § 1.14.4.A specifies 'Access (Transmission Facilities): A minimum 25-foot wide all-weather access route for vehicles to transmission easements with 16 feet minimum vertical clearance.' The regulatory overview defines transmission facilities as 'energized at 60kV or higher' and notes 'The 100-foot proximity threshold triggers specialized transmission review requirements.' The General Notes on Sheet 3 extensively reference transmission structures, transmission wires, and transmission easements with specific 25-foot requirements, strongly indicating that transmission infrastructure exists on or adjacent to the property. However, the site plan shows only 5-foot to 10-foot easement widths and provides no evidence of 25-foot access corridors. This creates a critical gap: either transmission facilities do not exist on the site (contradicting the extensive transmission notes), or the required 25-foot access corridors have not been shown on the plans. Without 25-foot access corridors clearly delineated and dimensioned on the plans, the applicant cannot demonstrate compliance with UCM § 1.14.4.A.
findings.comment: Minimum 25-foot wide all-weather access route for vehicles to transmission easements not provided or shown on plans. General Notes reference extensive transmission facility requirements (25-foot clearances, transmission structures, transmission wires), but no 25-foot transmission access corridors are shown or dimensioned on the Site Plan. Clarify the presence and location of transmission easements and facilities. If transmission easements exist, provide a clear delineation of the 25-foot minimum access corridor with 16-foot vertical clearance, all-weather paved surface (HMAC or PCC), and specifications for gates, grades, and curbs as required by UCM § 1.14.4.

applicableAreas: Transformer pad locations on west and east sides of the site
findings.observation: Vision analysis of Electrical Design Plan (Sheet 21) and Site Plan (Sheet 9) confirms: (1) Two pad-mounted transformer pads are clearly labeled and shown on the plans—one on the west side of the site south of Bldg. 1 and west of Bldg. 2, and one on the east side between Bldg. 5 and Bldg. 6. (2) A note on the electrical plan adjacent to the transformer pad reads exactly: 'need to look up approp. detail,' indicating the design is incomplete. (3) Vision analysis explicitly states: 'There is NO dimensioned access route explicitly drawn or labeled from the parking areas or public ROW to either transformer location.' (4) The analysis notes: 'Both transformers are sited immediately adjacent (visually within a few feet) to the internal drivable surface/parking aisle curbs. Exact distance dimensions from the curb to the pads are not provided.' (5) No dimensions are shown from parking areas or driveways to the transformer pads, and no specification confirms they are within 6 feet of drivable surfaces.
findings.reasoning: UCM § 1.3.16 requires 'Truck access to AE Construction and Existing Facility Sites' and specifies that 'Equipment pads: Within 6 feet of parking/traffic areas for truck accessibility.' UCM § 1.10.4 addresses 'Clearances from AE Padmount Equipment' and includes the requirement that transformer pads must have truck accessibility. The regulatory overview states 'Equipment pads: Within 6 feet of parking/traffic areas for truck accessibility.' The site plan must provide dimensioned evidence that each transformer pad is within 6 feet of a parking area or traffic surface capable of supporting bucket trucks. The incomplete detail notation ('need to look up approp. detail') and the absence of dimensions confirming the 6-foot proximity requirement constitute deficiencies. The applicant must provide specific dimensional verification of truck access to each pad.
findings.comment: 24/7 truck access to transformer locations not provided, shown on plans, or is obstructed by site improvements, fencing, or other features. Transformer pad locations are shown but access design is incomplete (noted as 'need to look up approp. detail'). No dimensioned access route from parking areas is provided, and distances from transformer pads to drivable surfaces are not verified. Provide detailed access plans for each transformer pad showing: (1) dimensioned distance from each pad to adjacent parking/traffic surfaces (must be within 6 feet), (2) surface specifications for access routes (HMAC or PCC pavement capable of supporting bucket truck weight), and (3) complete transformer pad detail that confirms truck accessibility for installation, operation, and maintenance.

applicableAreas: Underground electric ductbank routing areas throughout site
findings.observation: Vision analysis of Electrical Design Plan (Sheet 21) shows extensive blue lines labeled 'Underground Electric Line' throughout the site, indicating proposed underground electrical routing. However, the plan does not show specific ductbank details, pull box locations along the entire route, or designation of maintenance access pathways. Vision analysis notes: 'The proposed underground electrical routing (blue lines) traverses multiple surface types, passing beneath the main internal paved drive aisles, beneath concrete sidewalks, and through unpaved landscaped areas.' The plan shows pull boxes at some junctions but does not document whether maintenance access along the full length and width of the ductbank route is maintained and unobstructed. Building footprints and landscape features are shown in proximity to the proposed underground lines, but no specific analysis of ductbank access clearances is provided.
findings.reasoning: UCM § 1.3.16 requires truck access for maintenance of AE facilities, and UCM § 1.10.5 specifies clearances from underground facilities. Below-grade ductbanks require maintenance access along their entire length and width for Austin Energy personnel and equipment to inspect, repair, and replace conduits and cables. The applicant must demonstrate that buildings, hardscape, and permanent structures do not obstruct maintenance access to all below-grade ductbanks shown on the plans. Without detailed ductbank routing documentation and clearance analysis, it is unclear whether maintenance access will be maintained.
findings.comment: Access along the length and width to below-grade distribution ductbanks not maintained or shown for Austin Energy maintenance trucks and equipment. The Electrical Design Plan shows underground electric lines but does not provide detailed ductbank routing, pull box locations, or specification that maintenance access is maintained along the entire length and width. Provide a detailed underground ductbank plan showing: (1) complete ductbank routing with pull box locations, (2) clearances to buildings and permanent structures, and (3) designation of maintenance access pathways that remain unobstructed for truck and equipment access along the entire ductbank route.
